Question: Two boys \(A\) and \(B\) start at the same time to ride from Port Jervis to Poughkeepsie, \(60\) miles away. \(A\) travels \(4\) miles an hour slower than \(B.\) \(B\) reaches Poughkeepsie and at once turns back meeting \(A\) \(12\) miles from Poughkeepsie. The rate of \(A\) was:
Solution:
Method 1: Use the difference in total distances

At the meeting, \(A\) is \(12\) miles short of Poughkeepsie, so he has ridden \(60-12=48\) miles. Meanwhile, \(B\) has ridden \(60\) miles to Poughkeepsie and \(12\) miles back, for a total of \(72\) miles.

Both boys have been riding for the same elapsed time. Because \(B\) rides \(4\) miles farther in each hour, the difference in their total distances determines that time:
\[
\text{elapsed time}=\frac{72-48}{4}=6\text{ hours}.
\]
Thus \(A\)'s speed is \(48/6=8\) mph, choice \(\mathrm{B}\).

Method 2: Use the ratio of speeds

By the meeting, \(A\) has ridden \(60-12=48\) miles, while \(B\) has ridden \(60+12=72\) miles. Since their elapsed times are equal, their speeds have the same ratio as these distances:
\[
\text{speed of }A:\text{speed of }B=48:72=2:3.
\]
The difference between the speeds is therefore one ratio part. That part equals \(4\) mph, so \(A\)'s two parts equal \(2\cdot4=8\) mph, choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
